newsitem.title: USA: U.S. presents case in Japanese film market dispute.
newsitem.headline: U.S. presents case in Japanese film market dispute.

text.p: U.S. trade officials filed a complaint with the World Trade Organisation Thursday alleging that the Japanese government has attempted to thwart foreign entry into its photographic film and paper market.

In a 200-page, single spaced brief filed with a WTO dispute settlement panel, the United States said that for the last 30 years Japan imposed laws, regulations and administrative actions to strengthen its domestic industry and curtail opportunities for foreign firms.

"The government of Japan's intervention in reordering the conditions of competition in the photographic material industry has impaired market access for imports," U.S. Trade Representative Designate Charlene Barshefsky told a news conference.
"Moreover, at each stage of events, Japan has applied its commercial regulations for the express purpose of shielding domestic market leaders from import competition," she added.
She said the effect of those measures was to nullify and impair the benefits Japan's trading partners expected from tariff concessions made in international trade agreements.

"The record shows clearly at the very time that the government of Japan was liberalising its formal trade barriers on film and paper, it was undermining the effects of these changes by restructuring the domestic industry and imposing liberlization countermeasures to counteract the perceived advantages of foreign competitors," Barshefsky said.

"Essentially, Japan protected domestic enterprises in areas where they were most vulnerable to foreign competition until government policies had adequately shored up the domestic industry to meet that competition," she added.
She said the case was not a fight between two competitors -- Eastman Kodak Co. and Fuji Photo Film Co. Ltd -- but a trade dispute between two countries.
"This is a case about classic protectionism accomplished through novel means," Barshefsky said.
Lawyers for Fuji film denied the government of Japan deliberately acted to thwart foreign competition and said U.S. trade officials have failed to prove their case.
Fuji lawyers told reporters in a telephone conference that Kodak's problem in the Japanese market was a lack of demand, not impaired access.
A decision is not expected from the WTO until October.
